segments.title: Why the Leanders sit awkwardly between cruiser roles
segments.summary: The Leanders occupy the space between scout cruisers and first-class protected cruisers, so broad light-cruiser comparisons make their role look awkward.
segments.body: The criticism concerns role fit, while the Leanders are still described as attractive and capable ships. By the 1930s, the light-cruiser category had absorbed duties formerly divided among first- and second-class protected cruisers and scout cruisers. A design assessed against that combined category can appear weak at either end because it was built for something in between. In this reading, the Leanders make more sense as the equivalent of second-class protected cruisers than as pure scouts or first-class protected cruisers.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the class as a second-class protected-cruiser concept that sits between scout and first-class roles.

segments.title: A vanished cruiser role still shapes the design
segments.summary: The design preserves the logic of the old second-class protected cruiser even though that formal role had disappeared by the 1930s.
segments.body: When second-class protected cruisers were an accepted category, a ship could excel by filling that particular role. The formal role had disappeared by the 1930s, but the designers and admirals behind the new cruisers had learned their trade while it still existed. Their professional habits could survive the change in labels. The Leander concept shows how an obsolete classification could continue to shape a current design.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the old second-class protected-cruiser role with its disappearance in the 1930s and the influence of earlier professional experience.

segments.title: The Leander as a starting point for a cruiser programme
segments.summary: Starting again with a middle-of-the-road Leander allows a light-cruiser programme to develop toward either a larger first-class protected-cruiser type or a smaller scout.
segments.body: A middle-of-the-road design offers a sensible starting point for reviving a light-cruiser programme. It provides a base design before the navy commits to either end of the role spectrum. Enlarging it could lead toward a Town-class cruiser comparable to a first-class protected cruiser. Reducing it could produce a scout-cruiser type, with Arethusa offered as the closer comparison rather than Amphion. The Leander's value in this argument lies in its position at the centre of that design family, even though it does not define either extreme.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the Leander a sensible starting point and contrasts a larger Town-class direction with a reduced scout-cruiser direction.
